articles.title: AI agent swarms are a massive waste of tokens with zero quality gain, says OpenAI Codex developer
articles.summary: OpenAI Codex developer Eric Provencher warns that running more than two parallel sub-agents almost always burns tokens without improving quality because agents don't trust each other and end up double-checking everyone's work. He calls this the "coordination tax" and points to a project where 1,393 agents spent $20,000 in tokens on a single Python refactoring that one Astra agent could have handled for a fraction of the cost. articles.summary: Google Research has introduced Retrieve-for-Train (R4T), a framework for search that returns coherent, diverse result sets. It trains a fan-out language model with RL once, using groundedness, diversity, and alignment rewards. That model then synthesizes training data for a 53.9M-parameter diffusion retriever. The retriever generates all retrieval directions in a single pass, running 12× to 20× faster than autoregressive fan-out. No code or model weights have been released yet. articles.summary: I used to think the problem with junior developers was that they didn't know enough yet. Now I think the problem is they never get to be bad at something without someone finding out. Learning to code is mostly a long list of embarrassing guesses. You think the bug is in the database, it's in the loop. You think you understand recursion, you don't, not until the third time it breaks you. That ugly, wrong-guess phase is where the actual understanding gets built. Nobody skips it. Nobody ever has. Except now almost nothing stays unseen: The pull request gets reviewed before you've even decided if it's right The Slack thread gets a reaction before the idea is fully formed The pair programming session has someone watching your cursor The standup asks what you did yesterday, so yesterday has to sound like progress None of these are bad alone. The control is part of Cloudflare's Bot Management and AI Crawl Control toolbox, and it distinguishes among crawlers based on whether they search, train models, or act on behalf of users. The change matters because crawling is no longer one activity with one outcome. No finite collection of demonstrations can cover every task and situation a robot will encounter, making the ability to learn from context at deployment essential for generalization. articles.title: ReFigBench: Benchmarking Scientific Figure Reconstruction as Editable PowerPoint Artifacts
articles.summary: Multimodal coding agents are expected to turn visual inputs into usable artifacts, and they act through a harness, the layer of tools, context management, and execution environment around the model. Existing evaluations often isolate short tool calls, API traces, or screenshot resemblance, and a low score under these proxies cannot say whether the model saw poorly, planned poorly, or was failed by its harness. We study scientific overview figure reconstruction, an agent task in which a source image must become an editable PowerPoint slide that preserves text, topology, layout, and native document structure. We introduce ReFigBench, a benchmark and evaluation framework built on 1,000 real overview figures retrieved from arXiv papers with full provenance. Coding agents from four model families reconstruct every figure under two workflows, direct code generation and a specialized PPTX workflow, and the strongest model runs inside two commercial harnesses, yielding ten configurations. The code is at themsquared/k8s-agent-secrets-hardening.
